case_study_insert.main_stem: Caldera Geothermal Heat (CGH) is a cooperative in the renewable energy sector, employing a workforce of 34. Established in 2014 by community investors led by heat engineer Tomas Verhoeven, the cooperative operates the deep-borehole Caldera geothermal heat network, supplying district heating to 1,200 homes and St Anselm's Hospital. It works a flat structure governed democratically by an elected member board. CGH plans to invest $1,250,000 in a second heat exchanger station and 4 km of insulated pipework, financed by an $800,000 member share issue and $450,000 retained reserves. It has fixed costs of $630,000 a year, a variable cost of $78 a unit and a selling price of $120, and currently produces 27,000 units a year. CGH faces rising quality complaints about heat outages across its older connections.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Waste Report — Q3 2025: The network delivered 6,750 MWh of heat last quarter; 7% of connections reported outages, down from 11% a year ago. Average fault repair time fell to 4.6 hours. Customer complaints fell from 31 to 22 per month. A member survey of 1,200 households found 84% would support a tariff rise of $0.06 per unit to fund network expansion, and 59% chose CGH for environmental reasons. A skills audit shows 6 of 34 technicians have not completed high-pressure weld recertification (off-the-job training at the regional training centre costs $1,400 per technician; on-the-job training is constrained by the outage workload).

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing financing costs for infrastructure projects. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 7.1% from $12.70 to $13.60 per hour from April 2026, raising labour costs. (3) Construction materials inflation is running at 11.3%, and a government grant for renewable district-heating schemes will cover up to 30% of eligible project costs from 2027.

questions.question_text: CGH plans to finance the heat network expansion with an $800,000 member share issue and $450,000 retained reserves. Explain two advantages for CGH of using the member share issue instead of relying solely on retained reserves.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: An $800,000 member share issue raises far more expansion capital than the $450,000 of retained reserves alone, letting CGH fund the second heat exchanger station and 4 km of insulated pipework in full rather than scaling the project back. Deep-borehole geothermal assets are long-lived; member investors buying shares are essentially funding the community network that supplies 1,200 homes and St Anselm's Hospital, aligning their stake with the cooperative's mission.

Point 2: Share issues spread the financing burden across the membership instead of draining reserves earmarked for repairs and the rising outage complaints (7% of connections still fail). Instead of paying interest on a bank loan, CGH shares profits or surplus dividends with the households that own it, preserving the $630,000 a year fixed-cost cover and keeping tariffs affordable — the survey shows 84% of members would even accept a $0.06 per unit rise, giving the board room to price the service sustainably.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual explanation and analysis applied to Caldera Geothermal Heat and its expansion decision.

questions.question_text: CGH is launching its expanded heat network to St Anselm's Hospital and the homes along the 4 km pipework route. Consider community open days, local newspaper advertising, or targeted social media marketing to member households. Which should CGH choose to promote the expansion? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Community open days: Hosting site visits at the borehole and heat exchanger lets member households, St Anselm's Hospital estates staff and local councillors see geothermal engineering first-hand, building trust in a technology many people do not understand. Open days suit a cooperative's democratic culture — 59% of members already chose CGH for environmental reasons — and can convert sceptics into vocal advocates. However, they cost staff time and venue logistics for modest reach, and they attract mostly the already-engaged rather than new households in the 4 km extension zone.

Local newspaper advertising: Print adverts in the town's weekly paper would publicise lower bills and carbon-free heating to the extension area, reaching homeowners who do not follow CGH's channels. It is cheap per insertion and simple to book, but circulation has fallen, younger households rarely read print, response rates are hard to measure, and complex geothermal benefits cannot be explained well in a small advert.

Targeted social media marketing: Geo-targeted posts, videos of the heat exchanger and member testimonials can reach precisely the households inside the 4 km pipework route and the hospital's community, at low cost with measurable clicks, survey sign-ups and consultation attendance. They suit the 84% who would support a $0.06 per unit tariff rise and the environmentally motivated 59%, and allow CGH to run pre-launch consultations and FAQ sessions online. Risks include excluding less digitally connected elderly members and reliance on platform algorithms.

Recommendation: CGH should choose targeted social media marketing, supported by one well-publicised annual open day. Social media is the only option that reaches the right households at scale for a small workforce of 34, while honouring the cooperative's democratic consultation duty around the tariff rise. Community open days are rejected as the primary channel because of their limited reach beyond the already committed; local newspaper advertising is rejected as expensive per engaged household and weak for explaining geothermal benefits; the open day is retained as a trust-building complement, not the lead strategy.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotional options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of CGH with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of CGH with a well-justified recommendation explaining why community open days and newspaper advertising are rejected as lead channels.

questions.question_text: CGH faces rising quality complaints about heat outages, with 7% of connections still affected. Explain two benefits for CGH of using quality circles to involve its technicians in solving the outage problem.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Quality circles give CGH's 34 employees — especially the 6 technicians lacking weld recertification — a structured, voluntary forum to analyse outage causes and fault histories, using their hands-on knowledge of the network. Engaging the people who repair faults in under 4.6 hours surfaces root causes that managers miss, such as weld micro-fractures in older connections, directly attacking the 22 complaints per month and the $630,000 fixed-cost pressure.

Point 2: When technicians propose and pilot solutions themselves, they gain pride, ownership and skill development, satisfying esteem needs within the cooperative's flat, democratic structure. Successful quality circles lower the 7% outage rate, protect supply to St Anselm's Hospital, reduce emergency call-outs, and free staff for the $1,250,000 expansion project — improving reliability at a time when 84% of members already judge tariffs acceptable enough to back growth. Dependable repairs also strengthen the hospital's continuity planning confidence, which will matter when CGH negotiates the 2027 government grant towards the second heat exchanger station.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CGH's outages, complaints and expansion.

questions.question_text: CGH must recertify the 6 technicians whose high-pressure weld qualifications have lapsed. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the regional training centre. Which should CGH choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching beside the network's most experienced welders keeps repairs on the older connections moving while qualifications lapse, costs nothing in fees, and passes on CGH-specific knowledge of its borehole and pipework layouts. It protects output of 27,000 units a year and the 4.6-hour average repair time. However, CGH has no surplus senior welders while outages run at 7%, practice on live pressurised lines risks safety and further failures, and no recognised certificate is issued, which could breach insurer and hospital supply conditions.

Off-the-job training: The regional training centre course at $1,400 per technician costs $8,400 in total, gives structured high-pressure welding theory, safety drilling and a recognised certificate for all 6 technicians. Staff are away from the network during training, stretching the remaining crew, and course content may not match CGH's exact 4 km pipework alloys, so supervised on-site verification welds would still be required on return.

Decision: CGH should choose off-the-job training at the regional training centre, followed by supervised verification welds back on the network. High-pressure weld integrity is a safety and hospital-supply issue where an accredited certificate is non-negotiable; $8,400 is trivial against a $1,250,000 expansion, and the cooperative can absorb short absences by re-scheduling planned maintenance. On-the-job-only training is rejected because certifying welds practiced only on live, aging connections exposes residents and St Anselm's Hospital to failure and cannot produce the paperwork insurers demand; however, purely college-based delivery without on-site sign-off would leave CGH still uncertain about pipework-specific defects, so the combined approach is required.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to CGH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of CGH.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of CGH with a well-justified decision covering safety, cost, certification and network continuity.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how CGH's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $630,000 ÷ ($120 − $78) = $630,000 ÷ $42 = 15,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 15,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $120 − $78 = $42. Answer: contribution per unit is $42.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways CGH's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. CGH can compare its 15,000-unit break-even output with production of 27,000 units to confirm the heat network is profitable, with a margin of safety of 12,000 units, informing whether the new heat exchanger station can be financed without raising tariffs beyond the supported $0.06 rise.
2. Contribution per unit of $42 lets CGH model sensitivity to the proposed $0.06 tariff rise: extra revenue of $1,620 per 27,000 units ($0.06 × 27,000) flows almost entirely to surplus, which managers can weigh against member goodwill when consulting on the expansion vote.
3. Contribution data lets managers test the expansion's bankability: the second heat exchanger must generate enough unit sales to service the $800,000 member share issue obligations and $450,000 reserves committed, tying household connection targets directly to the business case for the 4 km pipework.
4. Unit cost data ($630,000 ÷ 27,000 units + $78 = $101.33 a unit) helps managers benchmark seasonal performance, identify waste behind the 7% outage rate and the 4.6-hour repair time, and negotiate energy and materials contracts as construction materials inflation runs at 11.3%.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 15,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $42 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 12,000 units vs 27,000-unit output; tariff-rise modelling with member consultation; share-issue feasibility for the $1,250,000 expansion; and unit-cost benchmarking at $101.33 to attack outages and waste.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate CGH's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, the profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has CGH's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 41.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 45.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 12.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 15.0%
ROCE 2024 = 16.0%
ROCE 2025 = 20.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 figures ($'000): gross profit $984,000 ÷ revenue $2,400,000 × 100 = 41.0%; 2025: gross profit $1,458,000 ÷ revenue $3,240,000 × 100 = 45.0%. Operating profit against revenue: 2024: $288,000 ÷ $2,400,000 × 100 = 12.0%; 2025: $486,000 ÷ $3,240,000 × 100 = 15.0%. Operating profit against capital employed: 2024: $288,000 ÷ $1,800,000 × 100 = 16.0%; 2025: $486,000 ÷ $2,430,000 × 100 = 20.0%. Cost of sales rose from $1,416,000 to $1,782,000 as heat volumes reached 27,000 units, but fell from 59.0% to 55.0% of revenue, and capital employed grew from $1,800,000 to $2,430,000 as the exchanger and pipework investment entered the accounts.

Evaluation: Profitability has strengthened decisively. Revenue grew 35.0% from $2,400,000 to $3,240,000, in step with the network delivering 6,750 MWh last quarter and winning households with the environmental case chosen by 59% of members. Gross profit improved from 41.0% to 45.0%, indicating tight control of the $78 variable cost per unit even with construction materials inflation at 11.3%. Operating profit improved from 12.0% to 15.0%, showing overheads absorbed the expansion well despite interest payable rising from $72,000 to $96,000. Operating profit against capital employed jumped from 16.0% to 20.0%, so the bigger asset base is working harder — a vital sign for a cooperative planning a $1,250,000 second heat exchanger station. Caution: member tariffs fund this growth, so CGH must honour its consultation promises and keep outages falling from 7% to protect trust; any sustained failure would hit both revenue and the democratic mandate.

Conclusion: CGH's financial performance has improved. Gross profit (41.0% to 45.0%), operating profit against revenue (12.0% to 15.0%) and operating profit against capital employed (16.0% to 20.0%) all rose, supported by a 35.0% revenue increase. Provided the outage rate keeps falling and the member consultation on the $0.06 tariff rise is handled openly, CGH is well placed to finance and operate the second station successfully.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether CGH's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for CGH of expanding its renewable geothermal heat network into the 4 km extension zone.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Extending the geothermal network to the 4 km extension zone and St Anselm's Hospital's wider estate gives CGH a captive, long-term customer base on one of the lowest-carbon heating sources available, reinforcing why 59% of members chose CGH for environmental reasons. Long contracts spread fixed costs of $630,000 a year across more units, lifting contribution from $42 and helping the cooperative leverage up to 30% of eligible project costs from the 2027 government grant, de-risking the $1,250,000 investment.

Disadvantage: The extension requires upfront trenching, pipework and heat exchanger spending at a time when construction materials inflation is running at 11.3%, so the final bill could exceed $1,250,000 and strain CGH's $450,000 retained reserves. Any delays would prolong the 7% outage problem on the older network, raise customer complaints further above 22 per month, and test member confidence in the $0.06 per unit tariff rise the board hopes to justify — undermining the democratic mandate if the new homes connect before older connections are reliable.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to CGH's finances, members and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the interest rate rise to 5.25%, the 7.1% minimum wage increase to $13.60 and the 11.3% construction materials inflation will affect CGH. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): CGH's $1,250,000 expansion is funded by a member share issue and retained reserves rather than a conventional bank loan, so direct interest exposure is limited to interest payable, which already rose from $72,000 to $96,000 in Appendix 2 — a 5.25% rate environment adds modestly to financing costs if any component is loan-based. Higher rates do make the alternative of bank finance less attractive, strengthening the case for the member issue, but the cash impact is small relative to a utility-scale project.

Minimum wage increase (7.1%, to $13.60 per hour): With a workforce of 34 technicians and support staff, a 7.1% rise adds roughly $1,900 per employee a year, or about $65,000 across the cooperative — meaningful against $486,000 of 2025 operating profit, and one that CGH can partly offset through the quality-circle productivity drive, the 4.6-hour repair-time gains and automation of metering.

Construction materials inflation (11.3%): Pipework, heat exchangers, insulation and trenching dominate the $1,250,000 expansion budget. An 11.3% rise on materials adds roughly $110,000–$130,000 to the project cost; even if the 2027 government grant covers 30% of eligible costs, the unfunded balance still rises, and pressure lands on the $800,000 member share issue and the $0.06 per unit tariff rise. Materials inflation also squeezes the $78 variable cost per unit of ongoing operations and maintenance.

Conclusion: The 11.3% construction materials inflation will have the greatest impact. It adds six figures directly to the expansion CGH is about to start, threatens to breach the member share issue envelope, and forces either a deeper tariff rise or delayed works on the 4 km pipework — striking the cooperative's core strategy rather than just its cost line. The minimum wage rise costs around $65,000 a year and is manageable through productivity; the interest rate rise is smallest in cash terms because CGH is largely member-funded; all three reinforce the need for early procurement and fixed-price contracts with suppliers.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to CGH.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on CGH's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of CGH with a well-justified judgment that construction materials inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
